subject: electrical-computer
audience: FE Electrical and Computer candidates and engineering students
title: The 8 Ohm Load That Became 128 Ohms
featured_title: THE 8 OHM LOAD THAT BECAME 128 OHMS

presentation.challenge: The secondary load was 8 Ω. The primary source did not see 8 Ω—or even 32 Ω.

practice.primary_question: Why is transformer reflected impedance proportional to the square of the turns ratio?
practice.typical_exam_trap: Multiplying load impedance by the turns ratio instead of the square of the turns ratio.

case_dna.target_misconception: A transformer reflects load impedance by the same linear turns ratio used for voltage.
case_dna.why_plausible: Voltage scales directly with turns ratio, so it is tempting to use the same factor for impedance.
case_dna.contradicting_evidence: With Np:Ns = 4:1 and ZL = 8 Ω, Zref = (4/1)²×8 = 128 Ω.
case_dna.corrected_model: Voltage scales as a, current scales inversely as 1/a, so impedance V/I scales as a².

problem_statement: An ideal transformer has Np:Ns = 4:1 and an 8 Ω resistive load on the secondary. A review note says the primary sees 32 Ω. With 120 V rms applied to the primary, measured primary current is about 0.94 A, corresponding to 128 Ω. Diagnose the turns-ratio error and verify voltage, current, and reflected impedance.

gates.label: Incident
gates.heading: The primary current was four times smaller than the 32 Ω model predicted.
gates.prompt: How should the 8 Ω load be reflected to the primary?

options.label: Zprimary = (Np/Ns)² Zload
options.reason: Impedance scales with the square of the turns ratio.

options.label: Zprimary = (Np/Ns) Zload
options.reason: That is voltage scaling, not impedance scaling.

options.label: An ideal transformer does not change impedance
options.reason: It reflects impedance by turns ratio squared.

gates.label: Predict
gates.heading: Predict the reflected load
gates.prompt: For a 4:1 turns ratio and an 8 Ω secondary load, what impedance (Ω) appears at the primary?

gates.label: Experiment
gates.heading: Measure primary current
gates.result: Primary current is about 0.94 A, consistent with 120 V / 128 Ω.

gates.label: Gap
gates.heading: Prove the reflected impedance
gates.prompt: Use Zref = (4/1)² × 8 Ω. Enter the primary-referred impedance.

gates.label: Evidence
gates.heading: Voltage and current ratios agree with 128 Ω

cards.text: Primary current is Is/4 = 0.9375 A, so 120/0.9375 = 128 Ω.

gates.label: Redline
gates.heading: Correct the transformer note
report: C2. The secondary load is 8 Ω.

claims.label: C3
claims.reason: Impedance uses the square of the ratio.

evidence_choices.label: (4)²×8 = 128 Ω and 120/128 = 0.9375 A
evidence_choices.reason: This matches the measured primary current.

correction.template: The 8 Ω secondary load reflects as {zref} Ω at the primary.

gates.label: Transfer
gates.heading: Apply reflected impedance
gates.prompt: An ideal 2:1 transformer has a 10 Ω secondary load. What impedance appears at the primary?

options.label: 20 Ω
options.reason: That uses the ratio only once.

options.label: 2.5 Ω
options.reason: That reflects in the wrong direction.

gates.explanation: Impedance referred from secondary to primary scales by (Np/Ns)².

gates.label: Sign Off
gates.heading: Sign off the transformer model
gates.confirmation: I confirm that ideal-transformer impedance reflection uses the square of the turns ratio.

items.label: What failed
items.value: The primary impedance was predicted as 32 Ω instead of 128 Ω.

items.label: What was assumed
items.value: Impedance was scaled linearly with turns ratio.

seo.seo_title: Transformer Reflected Impedance: Why 8 Ω Becomes 128 Ω | FE E-031
seo.meta_description: Solve FE Case E-031: a 4:1 ideal transformer makes an 8 Ω secondary load appear as 128 Ω at the primary. Learn the turns-ratio-squared rule.
seo.excerpt: Voltage scales with turns ratio, but impedance does not. An 8 Ω load can appear as 128 Ω through a 4:1 transformer.
seo.direct_answer: For an ideal transformer, impedance referred to the primary is Zp = (Np/Ns)² Zs. With a 4:1 turns ratio and an 8 Ω load, the primary sees 16×8 = 128 Ω.

faqs.q: How do you reflect impedance through an ideal transformer?
faqs.a: Multiply by the square of the turns ratio in the direction of reflection.

faqs.q: What does an 8 Ω load look like through a 4:1 transformer from the primary side?
